catalog_quote: 1.4 Word stress. Where words have light final syllables, Sula has penultimate stress (e.g. ['gɛ.hi] ‘back’), but stress is final in words with heavy final syllables (e.g. [ba.pi'kir] 'to think'). A moraic analysis (e.g. Trubetzkoy 1939) fits the Sula data well. In this analysis, closed syllables and open syllables with a diphthong or long vowel would be bimoraic, and stress would predictably fall on whichever syllable contains the penultimate mora. (62) [ba.'jon] 'mouth' compared to ['ba.ma] ‘to split/chop’ (63) [sa.'mam] 'to chew' compared to ['sa.ma] ‘same’ (64) [ba.ka.'lɛŋ] 'to lie down' compared to ['po.hi 'ka.ya] ‘grapefruit’ (65) [da.'gis] 'pain' compared to ['da.et] ‘branch’ ... In compound words, primary stress is located on the stressed syllable of the first stem, and subsequent stems are assigned secondary stress. (66) ['t˭ɛ.naˌlal] 'intestines' ... [p. 46:] Grammatical words …

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Bloyd 2020 PDF we hold/txt at sec. 1.4 (p. 215, compounds on p. 216) and is corroborated by the p. 46 overview and the p. 148 historical note; the classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, stress on syllable with penultimate mora, heavy = CVC and CVV incl. diphthong/long vowel, secondary stress only in compounds) matches the source exactly. Bloyd 2020 is the only grammar of Sula in Glottolog's full 11-item bibliography and no phonology article or instrumental study surfaced; Bloyd 2015 was downloaded and is silent. Only cosmetic fix: extend locator to pp. 215-216. Caveats worth keeping in mind but not changing the code: description is impressionistic, stress 'largely realized by vowel length' (p. 147), and some Mangon words with historically derived final long vowels show inter-speaker variation (p. 148). downloaded file and
